look_here_first: PHOTOGRAPH THE BASE before flowers: Texas sage is NOT a true rosette, but has basal leaves plus stem leaves. Basal leaves are narrowly elliptic to oblanceolate (~25–60 × 4–10+ mm); then look for terminal many-flowered raceme with leaflike bracts. Critical tiny confirmation is glandular hairs SUNKEN in pits on the foliage; Engelmann has elevated tack-shaped glands.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Taprooted perennial with woody caudex, usually short.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Both basal and cauline opposite leaves; basal blades narrow oblanceolate to elliptic.

key_traits.label: Surface
key_traits.text: Leaf surfaces have sunken/pitted glandular hairs.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: Terminal raceme with conspicuous leaflike bracts.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Joey's Borderlands podcast context places this sage in xeric scrub/limestone-hill country; use habitat as supporting context after checking the ribbed pointed calyx and pitted glandular hairs.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Basal AND cauline leaves (but NOT a true rosette)

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Leaflike pointed bracts and many-flowered terminal raceme

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Glandular hairs sunken in leaf pits (microscope/macro only)

key_traits.label: Joey field context
key_traits.text: A Borderlands podcast transcript normalizes Joey's spoken taxon to Salvia texana with high confidence and associates it with xeric scrub/limestone hills. The archive still flags an audio check as desirable, so this is kept as attributed habitat context rather than a new diagnostic character.
